ety.text: Old French veinebor. Middle English veine English vein From Middle English veine, borrowed from Anglo-Norman veine, from Latin vēna (“a blood-vessel; vein; artery”) of uncertain origin. See vēna for more. Doublet of vena. Displaced native edre, from ǣdre (whence edder).

senses.d: A blood vessel that transports blood from the capillaries back to the heart.
ex: The nurse hovered her vein finder to locate the veins in the patient's body.

senses.d: The entrails of a shrimp.
In leaves, a thickened portion of the leaf containing the vascular bundle.

A stripe or streak of a different colour or composition in materials such as wood, cheese, marble or other rocks.
A sheetlike body of crystallized minerals within a rock.
A topic of discussion; a train of association, thoughts, emotions, etc.
ex: He[…]is able to open new scenes, and discover a vein of true and noble thinking.

senses.d: A style, tendency, or quality.
ex: The play is in a satirical vein.
certain discoursing wits which are of the same veins

senses.d: A fissure, cleft, or cavity, as in the earth or other substance.
ex: down to the veins of earth
I took another Prism therefore which was free from Veins

senses.d: To mark with veins or a vein-like pattern.
ex: “We brought out our maps of the region and showed him the old routes and trails veining the whole of it. […]”

ety.text: From Middle English veil, veyl, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French veil (“sail, veil, shroud”) (Francien Old French voil, French voile), Latin vēlum (“cloth, covering”). Displaced Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyre (“veil”) (compare German Schleier). Doublet of velum and voile.

senses.d: Something hung up or spread out to hide or protect the face, or hide an object from view; usually of gauze, crepe, or similar diaphanous material.
ex: The veil of the temple was rent in twain.
She, as a veil down to the slender waist, / Her unadorned golden tresses wore.

senses.d: Anything that partially obscures a clear view.
A cover; disguise; a mask; a pretense.
ex: [I will] pluck the borrowed veil of modesty from the so seeming Mistress Page.
Beckett complains that "in the forest of symbols" there is never quiet, and longs to break through the veil of language to silence.

senses.d: A covering for a person or thing; as, a caul (especially over the head)
The calyptra of mosses.
velum (A circular membrane round the cap of a medusa).
A thin layer of tissue which is attached to or covers a mushroom.
A membrane connecting the margin of the pileus of a mushroom with the stalk; a velum.
ex: The genus Amanita has both a volva and a veil; the spores are white, and the stem is easily separable from the cap.

senses.d: An obscuration of the clearness of the tones in pronunciation.
That which separates the living and the spirit world.
ex: "I have heard most furious bigots talking through the veil." "So have I, for that matter," said Malone, "and in this very room."

senses.d: To dress in, or decorate with, a veil.
ex: Bedouin women veil their faces more strictly than city dwellers but enjoy greater freedom of dress and movement.

I'm under surface
Towers veiled in silk
I guess I'm not welcome
In this house they built

senses.d: To conceal as with a veil.
ex: The forest fire was veiled by smoke, but I could hear it clearly.
